ai_summary:
Scotland’s electricity system presents a stark operational paradox today, characterized by exceptional local renewable generation alongside acute cross-border transmission bottlenecks. Great Britain’s total wind output sits at 14.2 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 5.0 GW, representing 49.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this abundant clean generation, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, in sharp contrast to the 85 gCO2/kWh recorded GB-wide.

However, transmission network limitations severely restrict the flow of power across the Anglo-Scottish boundary. As a consequence, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 66.0 GWh through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a direct constraint cost of about £1,922,521. To replace this trapped low-carbon power, an estimated 12,534,205 m3 of gas had to be burned elsewhere on the network, generating an avoidable 23,089 tonnes of CO2.

Extrapolating these daily constraint expenditures suggests an estimated total yearly cost of approximately £702 million, which ultimately adds around £2.50/MWh onto electricity invoices for every consumer across the UK. This substantial economic and environmental burden underscores the critical need for accelerated transmission infrastructure investments to eliminate boundary bottlenecks and fully realize Scotland’s zero-carbon potential.
